6	
7	## Hydroxyl compounds — 4.4.1
8	
9	### Representing the alcohol families
10	
11	An alcohol has a hydroxyl group, –OH, attached to a saturated carbon. For an open-chain saturated molecule with one hydroxyl group and no other functional group, the general composition is CnH2n+2O, also written CnH2n+1OH. The hydrogen on oxygen is part of the total hydrogen count. This relationship does not apply without qualification to molecules containing rings, additional multiple bonds or several hydroxyl groups.
12	
13	Structural condensed notation CH3CH2OH makes ethanol's connections clear: two carbon atoms lead to O–H. A displayed drawing must show the C–O and O–H bonds, together with each C–H bond. In skeletal notation the carbon skeleton can omit carbon-bound hydrogen, but O and its attached H must remain explicit. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms answer different requests: a molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio, and the other forms retain connectivity.
14	
15	![Original displayed ethanol with explicit O–H](assets/8224-ethanol-displayed.png)
16	
17	The local environment of the carbon bearing OH distinguishes alcohol classes. CH3CH2OH is primary because that carbon has one carbon neighbour. CH3CH(OH)CH3 is secondary because it has two, while (CH3)3COH is tertiary because it has three. The oxygen has one bond to carbon and one to hydrogen in each example; classifying by oxygen's two bonds would not distinguish them.
18	
19	Keep branches and OH on their specified atoms when converting representations. In the tertiary example the central carbon has no attached H: it is bonded to three methyl carbons and oxygen. Drawing an additional H there would give five single bonds. Topic 4.1 supplies representation conventions, while the classification section below connects the OH-bearing carbon's attachments to oxidation behaviour.
20	
21	### Naming the hydroxyl position
22	
23	Choose the longest suitable chain containing the carbon attached to OH and use the ending –ol. Number from the end giving the hydroxyl group its lowest permitted locant. The one-to-six-carbon parent stems are meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent- and hex-. Methanol and ethanol have no distinct alternative hydroxyl position after equivalent end numbering. Longer chains can require a number: CH3CH2CH2OH is propan-1-ol and CH3CH(OH)CH3 is propan-2-ol.
24	
25	The locant belongs immediately before –ol in the naming style used here. For CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3, start numbering from the end nearer OH and obtain butan-2-ol. Butan-3-ol would describe the same connections with unnecessarily high numbering. Position is read from the molecular connections, not from which end happens to be printed on the left.
26	
27	Branches are included as prefixes with their own locants. (CH3)2CHCH2OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol: a three-carbon parent includes the OH-bearing carbon, and carbon 2 has a methyl substituent. (CH3)3COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Both contain four carbons altogether but differ in the OH-bearing carbon's attachments. The names distinguish those connections instead of merely announcing a total atom count.
28	
29	To check a name, draw the numbered parent, attach OH at the stated carbon and add the substituents. Complete valencies last, including O–H. Reconstructing propan-2-ol gives one hydrogen on the OH-bearing carbon, whereas reconstructing 2-methylpropan-2-ol gives none there. Naming and classification thus provide useful independent checks, but neither replaces the requested drawing or molecular count when a question asks for those forms. Topic 4.2 uses related locant reasoning for carbon–carbon double bonds.
30	
31	### Counting atoms without losing the OH hydrogen
32	
33	Count all carbon atoms, including methyl branches, then count oxygen and hydrogen separately. Carbon has four bond contributions; neutral alcohol oxygen has two single bonds, normally one to carbon and one to hydrogen. The hydrogen in OH can be overlooked when expanding a skeletal drawing, so include it explicitly in the final total. Classifying a molecule as primary, secondary or tertiary does not change this accounting method.
34	
35	For CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, two CH3 groups supply six hydrogen atoms, the OH-bearing CH supplies one, CH2 supplies two and OH supplies one. The total is ten, giving C4H10O. For (CH3)3COH, three methyl groups supply nine hydrogens and OH supplies one; the central carbon supplies none. The result is also C4H10O. Equal composition therefore does not prove equal connectivity or equal alcohol class.
36	
37	For a saturated open-chain alcohol with one OH, use CnH2n+2O as a check after reading the structure. With n=4 it predicts H10, matching both examples. This check cannot locate OH or distinguish a branched structure from an unbranched one. It is also not a replacement for reading additional functional groups if the given molecule contains them.
38	
39	A molecular formula states the actual numbers, while an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio. Structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms show connections in different detail. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal answers are therefore not interchangeable. In ethanol the molecular count C2H6O cannot be reduced further; this coincidence does not make the two definitions identical. Topic 1.1 develops composition from mass data. Here the evidence is the supplied connectivity, and a correct answer follows from completing each atom's allowed bonding.
40	
41	### Ethanol as a reaction hub
42	
43	Complete combustion is CH3CH2OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(g) for hot gaseous water. Ethanol can therefore act as a fuel. In substitution with hydrogen bromide under suitable heated acidic settings, CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O. The OH-derived group is replaced by bromine; this differs from replacing the hydrogen on oxygen in the reaction with sodium.
44	
45	With sodium, 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2O−Na+ + H2. The product is sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas. The carbon skeleton and C–O connection remain, while the O–H hydrogen is removed. The whole molecule does not become a sodium atom with an attached hydrocarbon, and OH− is not the stated organic product.
46	
47	Warm acidified dichromate(VI) oxidises ethanol. Controlled oxidation with removal of volatile ethanal as it forms gives CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O. Heating under reflux with excess oxidant permits further oxidation: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O. Acidified dichromate changes from orange towards green as it is reduced. Distillation removes the aldehyde; reflux returns volatile material so reaction can continue. The choice changes the intended organic endpoint.
48	
49	Dehydration eliminates water to give ethene: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O. Heating with concentrated sulfuric acid, around 170°C for this conventional preparation, supplies a suitable dehydration setting. Passing ethanol vapour over heated aluminium oxide is an alternative catalytic route. Merely naming dilute acid does not specify the concentrated-acid dehydration preparation. The concentration and heating distinguish the stated route from mixing ethanol with a dilute aqueous acid.
50	
51	Esterification with ethanoic acid gives CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH ⇌ CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O using an acid catalyst and heating. The ester is ethyl ethanoate. At fixed temperature, equilibrium means the reaction need not consume all starting material. Topic 4.7 develops ester structure and hydrolysis; here recognise the alcohol's role and preserve the balance in each reaction.
52	
53	For a stoichiometric example, the sodium equation shows that 0.200 mol ethanol produces at most 0.100 mol hydrogen when sodium is in excess and reaction is complete. Divide the alcohol amount by two because two O–H hydrogens combine to make each H2 molecule. The ratio follows the balanced equation, not the number of carbon atoms.
54	
55	### Classifying the carbon carrying OH
56	
57	Locate OH, then identify the carbon directly bonded to its oxygen. Count the carbon atoms directly attached to that carbon. One gives a primary alcohol, two a secondary alcohol and three a tertiary alcohol. This is a local count. The total length of the molecule and the number of hydrogens elsewhere in the chain do not determine the class. Methanol has no attached carbon group but is conventionally treated with primary alcohols for its oxidation behaviour.
58	
59	In CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, the OH-bearing carbon is at an end and touches one other carbon, so butan-1-ol is primary. In CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, that carbon touches two carbons, making butan-2-ol secondary. In (CH3)3COH, it touches three methyl carbons, making 2-methylpropan-2-ol tertiary. All three examples contain one OH group; “tertiary” does not mean three hydroxyl groups.
60	
61	The same local count shows how much hydrogen is attached to the OH-bearing carbon. A usual primary RCH2OH has two, a secondary R2CHOH has one, and a tertiary R3COH has none. These patterns help explain the simple oxidation outcomes: forming a carbonyl by removal of the O–H hydrogen and a hydrogen on the same carbon is possible for the first two types. The tertiary type lacks that second hydrogen.
62	
63	Practise circling the relevant carbon before assigning a class, particularly in branched structures. For (CH3)2CHCH2OH the branched carbon is not the OH-bearing carbon; the terminal CH2OH still makes it primary. This prevents a neighbouring branch from being mistaken for a tertiary alcohol centre. The next section applies the classification to distinguishing reactions, while Topic 4.6 develops the carbonyl products formed by oxidation.
64	
65	### Distinguishing alcohols by oxidation
66	
67	Warm a suitable alcohol with acidified dichromate(VI) in the school oxidation comparison. Primary and secondary alcohols reduce the oxidant as they are oxidised, so an orange-to-green change supports reaction. A tertiary alcohol normally does not undergo the corresponding mild oxidation because its OH-bearing carbon lacks hydrogen. This is a statement about the specified mild route, rather than a claim that severe oxidation could not break other bonds.
68	
69	A primary alcohol can give an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. For propan-1-ol, controlled oxidation produces propanal, CH3CH2CHO; further oxidation produces propanoic acid. Propan-2-ol gives propanone, CH3COCH3. Keeping the carbon skeleton intact provides a useful check on the oxidation products. An unexpected extra carbon in a proposed product would require an additional reagent or reaction not supplied here.
70	
71	Suppose samples A and B both change orange dichromate to green, while C does not under matched mild settings. This supports reactive primary or secondary structures for A and B and, among the stated alcohol candidates, a tertiary structure for C. It does not decide which of A and B is primary, because both types react. Additional identification of an aldehyde versus ketone product is required. Topic 4.6 develops the structures of those carbonyl products.
72	
73	State an observation separately from a conclusion. “Orange becomes green” is observable; “it is secondary” is a structural inference that needs adequate discrimination. To compare samples, match temperature, reagent concentration and observation time. A negative result from a cold mixture or insufficient mixing cannot be treated as an equally controlled comparison. The best distinguishing reaction is one whose different outcomes separate the actual candidate structures given, rather than a memorised colour change applied without checking what it distinguishes.
74	
75	### The alkaline iodine test identifies a local arrangement
76	
77	An alcohol containing CH3CH(OH)R can be oxidised under the alkaline iodine test to a methyl carbonyl arrangement and then form triiodomethane, CHI3. The positive observation is a yellow precipitate, not merely disappearance of iodine colour or a yellow solution. Triiodomethane is also called iodoform. Write its identity clearly: three iodines and one hydrogen are attached to its single carbon.
78	
79	Propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, and butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, have the required local arrangement and give positive results with warm alkaline aqueous iodine. Ethanol also gives the test: it is oxidised to ethanal, which has the required CH3CO– arrangement for the subsequent reaction. This special primary alcohol must not be rejected simply because the other familiar positive alcohol examples are secondary.
80	
81	Pentan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3, is secondary but lacks a methyl group directly attached to its OH-bearing carbon, so it does not give the corresponding positive alcohol test. Likewise, primary propan-1-ol lacks the required arrangement. Thus a positive result is not a general test for alcohols or even for all secondary alcohols. Inspect the local connections around OH rather than counting methyl groups somewhere else in the molecule.
82	
83	For an original discrimination, a four-carbon alcohol gives a yellow CHI3 precipitate and is known to be secondary. Butan-2-ol fits both pieces of evidence. The test alone would not have established a unique structure without those restrictions. Nor is the precipitate 2-iodobutane: the alcohol's entire chain has not simply had OH replaced by I. Topic 4.6 connects the test with carbonyl structure. Record reagent, warmth, the solid observation and its chemical identity before drawing the structural conclusion.
84	
85	### Why alcohols can act as solvents
86	
87	An alcohol combines a polar hydroxyl group with a hydrocarbon group. Its OH can form hydrogen bonds with water and compatible solutes, while its carbon-containing part provides interactions with less polar substances. This combination allows suitable alcohols to dissolve a range of materials that would not all dissolve equally well in water alone. Dissolution is explained through favourable solute–solvent interactions, not by assuming the alcohol chemically destroys each dissolved substance.
88	
89	Short-chain alcohols have a relatively large polar contribution and mix well with water. As the hydrocarbon portion becomes larger, its non-polar character becomes more influential and water solubility generally decreases within comparable alcohols. Consequently “contains OH” does not establish unlimited miscibility for an arbitrary long-chain alcohol. Both the molecule's structure and the identity of the solute need consideration.
90	
91	In cosmetics, a suitable alcohol can help dissolve selected ingredients and distribute them through a formulation; volatility can also assist drying after application. This explains a solvent role and does not assert that all alcohols are appropriate for skin products. In the syllabus's coal application, an alcohol-based solvent can extract compatible soluble sulfur-containing compounds into the solvent phase. Extraction transfers those compounds for later separation. It does not mean that all forms of sulfur, including insoluble mineral material, are removed just by dissolving coal in any alcohol.
92	
93	Suppose an invented materials laboratory observes that a selected sulfur-containing organic solute dissolves in its chosen alcohol but poorly in water. The supported explanation invokes the balance of polar and hydrocarbon interactions. The observation supplies no percentage removal for a whole coal sample, because that sample may contain other sulfur forms and an inaccessible solid matrix. Topic 1.3 explains hydrogen bonding; Topic 4.3 distinguishes chemical substitution from the physical separation involved here. A useful solvent claim names what is dissolved and the setting in which the solvent works.

This special primary alcohol must not be rejected simply because the other familiar positive alcohol examples are secondary.

Pentan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3, is secondary but lacks a methyl group directly attached to its OH-bearing carbon, so it does not give the corresponding positive alcohol test. Likewise, primary propan-1-ol lacks the required arrangement. Thus a positive result is not a general test for alcohols or even for all secondary alcohols. Inspect the local connections around OH rather than counting methyl groups somewhere else in the molecule.

For an original discrimination, a four-carbon alcohol gives a yellow CHI3 precipitate and is known to be secondary. Butan-2-ol fits both pieces of evidence. The test alone would not have established a unique structure without those restrictions. Nor is the precipitate 2-iodobutane: the alcohol's entire chain has not simply had OH replaced by I. Topic 4.6 connects the test with carbonyl structure. Record reagent, warmth, the solid observation and its chemical identity before drawing the structural conclusion.

### Why alcohols can act as solvents

An alcohol combines a polar hydroxyl group with a hydrocarbon group. Its OH can form hydrogen bonds with water and compatible solutes, while its carbon-containing part provides interactions with less polar substances. This combination allows suitable alcohols to dissolve a range of materials that would not all dissolve equally well in water alone. Dissolution is explained through favourable solute–solvent interactions, not by assuming the alcohol chemically destroys each dissolved substance.

Short-chain alcohols have a relatively large polar contribution and mix well with water. As the hydrocarbon portion becomes larger, its non-polar character becomes more influential and water solubility generally decreases within comparable alcohols. Consequently “contains OH” does not establish unlimited miscibility for an arbitrary long-chain alcohol. Both the molecule's structure and the identity of the solute need consideration.

In cosmetics, a suitable alcohol can help dissolve selected ingredients and distribute them through a formulation; volatility can also assist drying after application. This explains a solvent role and does not assert that all alcohols are appropriate for skin products. In the syllabus's coal application, an alcohol-based solvent can extract compatible soluble sulfur-containing compounds into the solvent phase. Extraction transfers those compounds for later separation. It does not mean that all forms of sulfur, including insoluble mineral material, are removed just by dissolving coal in any alcohol.

Suppose an invented materials laboratory observes that a selected sulfur-containing organic solute dissolves in its chosen alcohol but poorly in water. The supported explanation invokes the balance of polar and hydrocarbon interactions. The observation supplies no percentage removal for a whole coal sample, because that sample may contain other sulfur forms and an inaccessible solid matrix. Topic 1.3 explains hydrogen bonding; Topic 4.3 distinguishes chemical substitution from the physical separation involved here. A useful solvent claim names what is dissolved and the setting in which the solvent works.

5	---
6	
7	## Isomerism: structural and stereoisomerism — 4.5
8	
9	### Enumerating structures systematically
10	
11	Begin with the molecular composition and any class restriction in the question. The same atom count can sometimes describe several families, so “all isomers” needs the stated scope. A molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio; structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms reveal connectivity. Keep these molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations distinct while checking that a proposed drawing has the required atom count.
12	
13	For C4H10 as an open-chain alkane, arrange four carbons first in an unbranched route and then in a branched skeleton. The distinct possibilities are butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, and 2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CH. Fill hydrogens to valency four. Drawing butane in a different zigzag or reversing its left-to-right order does not create another connectivity. The two names make it easier to detect duplicate drawings.
14	
15	For C4H8 restricted to open-chain alkenes with one double bond, use an unbranched four-carbon skeleton and move C=C between inequivalent positions. This gives but-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH3, and but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Putting the bond at the opposite terminal end repeats but-1-ene. A branched skeleton supplies 2-methylpropene, CH2=C(CH3)2. These are three structural connectivities. Saturated rings are outside this particular question's stated open-chain restriction, rather than being impossible with C4H8.
16	
17	Now inspect each connectivity for spatial alternatives. But-2-ene has cis and trans forms; the other two have a double-bond carbon with identical attachments and do not give this pair. Thus there are four distinct alkene forms when those two are counted separately. Record whether your total counts connectivities or includes stereoisomers. Check atom numbers, valencies, parent names and duplication at each stage. Topic 4.2 provides naming and composition tools; the later sections here explain the spatial test used in this enumeration.
18	
19	### Three kinds of structural isomerism
20	
21	Structural isomers have the same molecular composition but a different arrangement of connections between atoms. Chain isomerism changes the carbon skeleton. Butane and 2-methylpropane both contain four carbons and ten hydrogens, but the first has an unbranched route and the second a carbon attached to three methyl groups. Their difference is not merely that one drawing looks straighter on a page.
22	
23	Positional isomerism keeps the basic carbon skeleton and functional-group type but changes the position of a group or multiple bond. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol both have three-carbon chains and one OH, but OH is attached at an end in one and at the middle carbon in the other. But-1-ene and but-2-ene supply the corresponding double-bond example. Both members of each pair have matching total atom counts.
24	
25	Functional-group isomerism changes the functional group while retaining total composition. Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and methoxymethane, CH3OCH3, both have C2H6O. One has an O–H bond as an alcohol; the other has C–O–C connectivity as an ether. This example identifies a family difference; it does not require learning an extra ether reaction scheme. The oxygen's position among the connections supplies the distinguishing evidence.
26	
27	To assign a type, compare the carbon skeleton, then the functional group and its position. A change in the way a molecule is oriented in space without changing which atoms bond belongs to another comparison. Turning a sheet upside down or rotating a flexible single bond can produce a different-looking sketch of the same compound. Name both drawings and trace each atom's neighbours before counting them separately. A matching molecular atom count is necessary for an isomer pair, but is insufficient: two identical drawings after reorientation also have matching counts. Topic 4.1's functional-group vocabulary helps identify what has actually changed.
28	
29	For a final duplicate check, label the carbon atoms temporarily and follow the route between branch points or functional groups. Two sketches that can be matched atom for atom with the same neighbours represent one connectivity, even if one has been bent on the page. Remove the temporary labels before giving the chemical structure. By contrast, moving OH from an end carbon to an internal carbon changes its neighbours and gives a positional pair. This method keeps visual appearance separate from the evidence used to classify the isomers.
30	
31	### Same connections, different arrangement in space
32	
33	Stereoisomers have the same structural connections but a different arrangement of atoms in space. They also have the same molecular composition. The two divisions used here are geometrical, or cis–trans, isomerism and optical isomerism. A spatial difference must survive attempts to rotate the entire molecule into coincidence; a different viewing angle is not by itself a new stereoisomer.
34	
35	In but-2-ene the two methyl groups can lie on the same side of C=C or opposite sides. Both structures have the same sequence CH3–CH=CH–CH3. Nothing has been moved from one carbon to another, so this is not positional isomerism. They differ in the arrangement held by the double bond: cis has the methyl groups on the same side and trans has them on opposite sides.
36	
37	![Original cis and trans but-2-ene drawings](assets/8224-cis-trans-butene.png)
38	
39	Optical isomers in the simple one-centre examples are a pair of non-superimposable mirror images, called enantiomers. A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups provides a common source. A pure member can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light; the corresponding pure mirror form rotates it equally in the opposite direction under matched settings. Equal amounts of the two can cancel the net rotation. This cancellation concerns the sample, not disappearance of the chiral centres in its molecules.
40	
41	The diagnostic questions differ. For cis–trans, inspect C=C and compare attachments at each end. For the optical examples, inspect a tetrahedral centre and compare its four groups. Do not label any two differently drawn molecules “optical” merely because they have the same counts. Likewise, a cis–trans pair is not automatically a mirror-image pair. The following sections develop the restricted-rotation and four-different-groups tests without adding a new stereochemical naming system.
42	
43	### Restricted rotation makes cis and trans distinct
44	
45	A carbon–carbon double bond prevents the free rotation characteristic of a simple carbon–carbon single bond. Twisting the two alkene ends relative to one another would disrupt the π bonding interaction and requires a substantial energy input. Under ordinary settings the cis and trans structures therefore remain distinct rather than continuously exchanging through easy rotation about intact C=C.
46	
47	Restriction alone is not enough to give two distinguishable forms. Each double-bond carbon must have two different attached groups. But-2-ene meets that test: each carbon has H and CH3. The methyl groups can be on the same side, cis, or opposite sides, trans. In propene, one double-bond carbon has two H atoms. Interchanging those identical hydrogens gives the same arrangement, so propene does not form a cis/trans pair. Likewise CH2=C(CH3)2 fails the test at its CH2 end and at its two-methyl end.
48	
49	When drawing the but-2-ene pair, put C=C horizontally, give each carbon one H and one CH3, and keep three bonding directions around each alkene carbon. In the cis drawing both methyl labels are above, or both below, the double bond. In trans one is above and the other below. Reversing the entire drawing does not convert cis to trans, because the same-side or opposite-side relationship is unchanged.
50	
51	Avoid saying simply that cis–trans is caused by molecules being unable to move. Molecules can translate, rotate as whole objects and rotate around other bonds; the relevant constraint is relative rotation about the double bond. That is why a freely rotating butane sketch does not supply an analogous isolable pair just by showing its methyl groups in two positions on paper. Topic 4.1 describes local planar alkene geometry, and Topic 4.2 supplies the names used to identify which bond is under discussion.
52	
53	### A tetrahedral centre with four different groups
54	
55	A chiral centre in the carbon examples taught here is a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups. The groups need not begin with four different elements: two can both begin with carbon but differ farther along their connections. For butan-2-ol, the OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3. These are four different groups, making that carbon a chiral centre.
56	
57	Its mirror image has the same atom connections but cannot be placed on the original so that all four groups coincide by rotating the whole molecule. A simple pair of such non-superimposable mirror images gives optical isomerism. A wedge represents a bond towards the viewer, a hashed bond one away, and ordinary lines bonds in the page. A flat four-arm cross without a depth convention does not demonstrate the tetrahedral mirror relationship adequately.
58	
59	![Original mirror-image butan-2-ol centres](assets/8224-optical-mirror-pair.png)
60	
61	Propan-2-ol does not have this centre because its OH-bearing carbon has two identical methyl groups. A CH2 carbon also has two identical H atoms. Neither becomes chiral simply because the other two groups look different. In a candidate with a longer branch, trace each attached group far enough to decide whether it is genuinely different. The plus or minus sign for measured light rotation cannot be assigned from a wedge drawing by guessing which group lies to the right.
62	
63	Some molecules contain more than one chiral centre. Identify each candidate locally by its four attachments, but do not assume that the count of centres alone completely describes the whole molecule's optical behaviour. The syllabus does not require a fuller multi-centre classification. The essential transfer here is to inspect actual connections and show depth correctly in a one-centre pair. Topic 4.4 supplies the alcohol structures used in these examples; the centre remains a geometric property rather than a separate alcohol reaction.
64	
65	### Applying both structural tests
66	
67	Use two separate inspection routes on a supplied structure. First mark each C=C and inspect the two groups attached at each end. If either end has identical groups, the simple geometrical pair is absent at that bond. If both ends have different groups, the relevant same-side and opposite-side arrangements can be considered where the cis/trans description is unambiguous. Do not infer this property merely from the appearance of two parallel bond lines.
68	
69	Second inspect tetrahedral carbons. A carbon carrying two H atoms fails the four-different-groups test immediately. A carbon with four different attachments is a candidate chiral centre; mark that atom with an asterisk and identify the groups. The alkene carbons themselves have three attachment directions and are not the tetrahedral centres in this test. Thus the presence of a double bond does not automatically establish a chiral carbon.
70	
71	For CH3CH=CHCH(OH)CH2CH3, the C=C carbons each have one H and one different carbon-containing group, so geometrical alternatives are possible. The OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, an ethyl group and an unsaturated three-carbon group. Those attachments are different, making it a chiral centre. The example illustrates that both kinds of structural feature can occur in one molecule without requiring a complete catalogue of its spatial forms.
72	
73	By contrast, CH2=CHCH2OH has a terminal CH2 at the double bond and a CH2OH carbon. It fails the geometrical test because one alkene end has two H, and it fails the tetrahedral test because the alcohol carbon also has two H. State the specific duplicated group when rejecting a candidate. This is more informative than saying that the molecule is “too small” or “not symmetrical enough”. Throughout, preserve atom connections before discussing space: a change in OH position or carbon skeleton would create a structural comparison rather than a different arrangement of the same connections.

A molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio; structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms reveal connectivity. Keep these molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations distinct while checking that a proposed drawing has the required atom count.

For C4H8 restricted to open-chain alkenes with one double bond, use an unbranched four-carbon skeleton and move C=C between inequivalent positions. These are three structural connectivities. Saturated rings are outside this particular question's stated open-chain restriction, rather than being impossible with C4H8.

Now inspect each connectivity for spatial alternatives. But-2-ene has cis and trans forms; the other two have a double-bond carbon with identical attachments and do not give this pair. Thus there are four distinct alkene forms when those two are counted separately. Record whether your total counts connectivities or includes stereoisomers. Check atom numbers, valencies, parent names and duplication at each stage. Topic 4.2 provides naming and composition tools; the later sections here explain the spatial test used in this enumeration.

### Three kinds of structural isomerism

Structural isomers have the same molecular composition but a different arrangement of connections between atoms. Chain isomerism changes the carbon skeleton. Butane and 2-methylpropane both contain four carbons and ten hydrogens, but the first has an unbranched route and the second a carbon attached to three methyl groups. Their difference is not merely that one drawing looks straighter on a page.

Positional isomerism keeps the basic carbon skeleton and functional-group type but changes the position of a group or multiple bond. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol both have three-carbon chains and one OH, but OH is attached at an end in one and at the middle carbon in the other. But-1-ene and but-2-ene supply the corresponding double-bond example. Both members of each pair have matching total atom counts.

Functional-group isomerism changes the functional group while retaining total composition. Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and methoxymethane, CH3OCH3, both have C2H6O. One has an O–H bond as an alcohol; the other has C–O–C connectivity as an ether. This example identifies a family difference; it does not require learning an extra ether reaction scheme. The oxygen's position among the connections supplies the distinguishing evidence.

To assign a type, compare the carbon skeleton, then the functional group and its position. A change in the way a molecule is oriented in space without changing which atoms bond belongs to another comparison. Turning a sheet upside down or rotating a flexible single bond can produce a different-looking sketch of the same compound. Name both drawings and trace each atom's neighbours before counting them separately. A matching molecular atom count is necessary for an isomer pair, but is insufficient: two identical drawings after reorientation also have matching counts. Topic 4.1's functional-group vocabulary helps identify what has actually changed.

For a final duplicate check, label the carbon atoms temporarily and follow the route between branch points or functional groups. Two sketches that can be matched atom for atom with the same neighbours represent one connectivity, even if one has been bent on the page. Remove the temporary labels before giving the chemical structure. By contrast, moving OH from an end carbon to an internal carbon changes its neighbours and gives a positional pair. This method keeps visual appearance separate from the evidence used to classify the isomers.

### Same connections, different arrangement in space

Stereoisomers have the same structural connections but a different arrangement of atoms in space. They also have the same molecular composition. The two divisions used here are geometrical, or cis–trans, isomerism and optical isomerism. A spatial difference must survive attempts to rotate the entire molecule into coincidence; a different viewing angle is not by itself a new stereoisomer.

In but-2-ene the two methyl groups can lie on the same side of C=C or opposite sides. Both structures have the same sequence CH3–CH=CH–CH3. Nothing has been moved from one carbon to another, so this is not positional isomerism. They differ in the arrangement held by the double bond: cis has the methyl groups on the same side and trans has them on opposite sides.

![Original cis and trans but-2-ene drawings](assets/8224-cis-trans-butene.png)

Optical isomers in the simple one-centre examples are a pair of non-superimposable mirror images, called enantiomers. A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups provides a common source. A pure member can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light; the corresponding pure mirror form rotates it equally in the opposite direction under matched settings. Equal amounts of the two can cancel the net rotation. This cancellation concerns the sample, not disappearance of the chiral centres in its molecules.

The diagnostic questions differ. For cis–trans, inspect C=C and compare attachments at each end. For the optical examples, inspect a tetrahedral centre and compare its four groups. Do not label any two differently drawn molecules “optical” merely because they have the same counts. Likewise, a cis–trans pair is not automatically a mirror-image pair. The following sections develop the restricted-rotation and four-different-groups tests without adding a new stereochemical naming system.

### Restricted rotation makes cis and trans distinct

A carbon–carbon double bond prevents the free rotation characteristic of a simple carbon–carbon single bond. Twisting the two alkene ends relative to one another would disrupt the π bonding interaction and requires a substantial energy input. Under ordinary settings the cis and trans structures therefore remain distinct rather than continuously exchanging through easy rotation about intact C=C.

Restriction alone is not enough to give two distinguishable forms. Each double-bond carbon must have two different attached groups. But-2-ene meets that test: each carbon has H and CH3. The methyl groups can be on the same side, cis, or opposite sides, trans. In propene, one double-bond carbon has two H atoms. Interchanging those identical hydrogens gives the same arrangement, so propene does not form a cis/trans pair. Likewise CH2=C(CH3)2 fails the test at its CH2 end and at its two-methyl end.

When drawing the but-2-ene pair, put C=C horizontally, give each carbon one H and one CH3, and keep three bonding directions around each alkene carbon. In the cis drawing both methyl labels are above, or both below, the double bond. In trans one is above and the other below. Reversing the entire drawing does not convert cis to trans, because the same-side or opposite-side relationship is unchanged.

Avoid saying simply that cis–trans is caused by molecules being unable to move. Molecules can translate, rotate as whole objects and rotate around other bonds; the relevant constraint is relative rotation about the double bond. That is why a freely rotating butane sketch does not supply an analogous isolable pair just by showing its methyl groups in two positions on paper. Topic 4.1 describes local planar alkene geometry, and Topic 4.2 supplies the names used to identify which bond is under discussion.

### A tetrahedral centre with four different groups

A chiral centre in the carbon examples taught here is a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups. The groups need not begin with four different elements: two can both begin with carbon but differ farther along their connections. For butan-2-ol, the OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3. These are four different groups, making that carbon a chiral centre.

Its mirror image has the same atom connections but cannot be placed on the original so that all four groups coincide by rotating the whole molecule. A simple pair of such non-superimposable mirror images gives optical isomerism. A wedge represents a bond towards the viewer, a hashed bond one away, and ordinary lines bonds in the page. A flat four-arm cross without a depth convention does not demonstrate the tetrahedral mirror relationship adequately.

![Original mirror-image butan-2-ol centres](assets/8224-optical-mirror-pair.png)

Propan-2-ol does not have this centre because its OH-bearing carbon has two identical methyl groups. A CH2 carbon also has two identical H atoms. Neither becomes chiral simply because the other two groups look different. In a candidate with a longer branch, trace each attached group far enough to decide whether it is genuinely different. The plus or minus sign for measured light rotation cannot be assigned from a wedge drawing by guessing which group lies to the right.

Some molecules contain more than one chiral centre. Identify each candidate locally by its four attachments, but do not assume that the count of centres alone completely describes the whole molecule's optical behaviour. The syllabus does not require a fuller multi-centre classification. The essential transfer here is to inspect actual connections and show depth correctly in a one-centre pair. Topic 4.4 supplies the alcohol structures used in these examples; the centre remains a geometric property rather than a separate alcohol reaction.

### Applying both structural tests

Use two separate inspection routes on a supplied structure. First mark each C=C and inspect the two groups attached at each end. If either end has identical groups, the simple geometrical pair is absent at that bond. If both ends have different groups, the relevant same-side and opposite-side arrangements can be considered where the cis/trans description is unambiguous. Do not infer this property merely from the appearance of two parallel bond lines.

Second inspect tetrahedral carbons. A carbon carrying two H atoms fails the four-different-groups test immediately. A carbon with four different attachments is a candidate chiral centre; mark that atom with an asterisk and identify the groups. The alkene carbons themselves have three attachment directions and are not the tetrahedral centres in this test. Thus the presence of a double bond does not automatically establish a chiral carbon.

For CH3CH=CHCH(OH)CH2CH3, the C=C carbons each have one H and one different carbon-containing group, so geometrical alternatives are possible. The OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, an ethyl group and an unsaturated three-carbon group. Those attachments are different, making it a chiral centre. The example illustrates that both kinds of structural feature can occur in one molecule without requiring a complete catalogue of its spatial forms.

By contrast, CH2=CHCH2OH has a terminal CH2 at the double bond and a CH2OH carbon. It fails the geometrical test because one alkene end has two H, and it fails the tetrahedral test because the alcohol carbon also has two H. 1	# 4.6 Carbonyl compounds
2	
3	*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Carbonyl compounds — 4.6.1
8	
9	### Aldehyde and ketone connections
10	
11	A carbonyl group is C=O. In an aldehyde its carbon has at least one attached hydrogen, giving the group –CHO at the end of an open chain. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon groups, giving –CO– within a carbon skeleton. Methanal, HCHO, is the simplest aldehyde and has two H attached to the carbonyl carbon; a ketone needs at least three carbons to provide its two carbon attachments.
12	
13	For saturated open-chain molecules containing one carbonyl and no other functional group, the general composition is CnH2nO. Propanal, CH3CH2CHO, and propanone, CH3COCH3, both have C3H6O. The count therefore does not decide whether the compound is an aldehyde or ketone. Connectivity supplies that distinction.
14	
15	Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms describe different information. A molecular formula gives actual counts and an empirical formula their simplest ratio. Structural condensed notation retains grouped connections; a displayed drawing shows each bond; skeletal notation omits carbon labels and their hydrogen while retaining the oxygen and C=O double line. In condensed –CHO, the H is attached to carbon, not to oxygen. Do not read CHO as an alcohol OH group.
16	
17	![Original aldehyde and ketone carbonyl connections](assets/8224-carbonyl-connections.png)
18	
19	Each carbonyl carbon has four bond contributions: two to oxygen and two single-bond attachments. The oxygen has its double bond and no implied O–H hydrogen. Check these details when expanding a skeletal representation. Topic 4.1 explains planar geometry at a carbonyl carbon and infrared carbonyl absorption; Topic 4.4 distinguishes the alcohol C–OH arrangement from the oxidised C=O arrangement.
20	
21	### Names include the carbonyl carbon
22	
23	Aldehydes use the ending –al. Select a parent chain containing the CHO carbon and include that carbon in the chain count. It is carbon 1, so CH3CH2CHO is propanal, not ethanal with an extra unnamed group. The one-to-six-carbon straight-chain aldehydes are methanal, ethanal, propanal, butanal, pentanal and hexanal. Branch locants are counted from the aldehyde end.
24	
25	For example, CH3CH(CH3)CHO is 2-methylpropanal. Its parent has three carbons including CHO, while the methyl substituent adds a fourth to the whole molecule. Reconstructing the name gives the same carbon skeleton and ensures that an H remains attached to the carbonyl carbon. Merely naming the longest chain anywhere in a branched drawing can be wrong if that route omits the aldehyde group.
26	
27	Ketones use –one and number the parent from the end giving the carbonyl carbon its lowest permitted locant. CH3COCH2CH2CH3 is pentan-2-one. CH3CH2COCH2CH3 is pentan-3-one. Both parents contain five carbons; the number identifies which carbon bears =O. In propanone there is one possible internal carbonyl position, so its usual simple name needs no locant.
28	
29	To reverse a ketone name, draw the complete parent carbon chain first, number it and add a double bond to oxygen at the named carbon. Then fill the remaining carbon valencies with hydrogen. A terminal carbon bearing =O and H would instead give an aldehyde structure. Naming is therefore tied to connections, rather than a choice of ending based solely on a total atom count. Topic 4.5 uses this difference when identifying functional-group structural isomers.
30	
31	### Composition from a carbonyl drawing
32	
33	Count the carbonyl carbon as part of the carbon skeleton, then complete valencies at each carbon. Its double bond to O uses two contributions. In an aldehyde, one remaining contribution can be C–H and the other C–C; in a ketone both remaining contributions are C–C. Oxygen does not carry an implicit hydrogen in C=O. This is a common difference from the alcohol structures used earlier.
34	
35	For CH3CH2CH2CHO, the hydrogen total is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, so butanal has C4H8O. For CH3COCH2CH3, the methyl groups supply six H, CH2 supplies two and the carbonyl carbon none, again giving C4H8O. Thus the same count can belong to an aldehyde or a ketone. The molecular composition does not establish the name or structure without further evidence.
36	
37	In a skeletal drawing, a line to an explicit oxygen label is not an extra carbon position. The two lines of C=O represent a double bond between one carbon and one oxygen, not two oxygen atoms. Counting line strokes instead of labelled atoms and carbon positions would therefore give an impossible composition.
38	
39	Use the saturated open-chain CnH2nO relationship as a check after the direct count. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms are separate answers: a molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula a ratio, and the connection representations show where atoms attach. Topic 1.1 covers calculating relative molecular mass from those counts. Here a calculated Mr can confirm arithmetic but cannot distinguish two isomers with equal composition.
40	
41	### Preparing carbonyls from alcohols
42	
43	Use acidified dichromate(VI), Cr2O7²−/H+, to oxidise primary and secondary alcohols. Ethanol gives ethanal in controlled oxidation: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O. The primary alcohol loses hydrogen from OH and from the same carbon to form C=O. Further oxidation can produce ethanoic acid, so limiting the intended stage and removing the volatile aldehyde as it forms helps obtain the aldehyde product.
44	
45	A secondary alcohol instead gives a ketone. Propan-2-ol gives propanone: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O. Its OH-bearing carbon has one H available for removal and two carbon attachments. The product retains those two attachments at the carbonyl carbon. Oxidation of butan-2-ol similarly gives butan-2-one, preserving four carbons and the carbonyl position corresponding to the original OH-bearing carbon.
46	
47	The oxidant's orange colour changes towards green as dichromate(VI) is reduced. That observation supports oxidation but does not on its own identify which carbonyl formed, since both primary and secondary alcohols can react. Use the starting alcohol's connections and product structure as well. A tertiary alcohol lacks H on its OH-bearing carbon and resists this ordinary mild carbonyl-forming route.
48	
49	For a worked amount calculation, 0.100 mol propan-2-ol can give at most 0.100 mol propanone if oxidation is complete: the organic ratio is 1:1. Mr(propanone)=3(12.0)+6(1.0)+16.0=58.0, so the corresponding mass is 5.80 g. Actual isolated yield can be lower through incomplete reaction or loss during separation; neither changes the stoichiometric maximum calculated from the balanced equation. Topic 4.4 teaches the alcohol reaction map, and Topic 4.7 develops the carboxylic-acid endpoint of further primary oxidation.
50

## Carbonyl compounds — 4.6.1

### Aldehyde and ketone connections

A carbonyl group is C=O. In an aldehyde its carbon has at least one attached hydrogen, giving the group –CHO at the end of an open chain. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon groups, giving –CO– within a carbon skeleton. Methanal, HCHO, is the simplest aldehyde and has two H attached to the carbonyl carbon; a ketone needs at least three carbons to provide its two carbon attachments.

For saturated open-chain molecules containing one carbonyl and no other functional group, the general composition is CnH2nO. Propanal, CH3CH2CHO, and propanone, CH3COCH3, both have C3H6O. The count therefore does not decide whether the compound is an aldehyde or ketone. Connectivity supplies that distinction.

Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms describe different information. A molecular formula gives actual counts and an empirical formula their simplest ratio. Structural condensed notation retains grouped connections; a displayed drawing shows each bond; skeletal notation omits carbon labels and their hydrogen while retaining the oxygen and C=O double line. In condensed –CHO, the H is attached to carbon, not to oxygen. Do not read CHO as an alcohol OH group.

![Original aldehyde and ketone carbonyl connections](assets/8224-carbonyl-connections.png)

Each carbonyl carbon has four bond contributions: two to oxygen and two single-bond attachments. The oxygen has its double bond and no implied O–H hydrogen. Check these details when expanding a skeletal representation. Topic 4.1 explains planar geometry at a carbonyl carbon and infrared carbonyl absorption; Topic 4.4 distinguishes the alcohol C–OH arrangement from the oxidised C=O arrangement.

### Names include the carbonyl carbon

Aldehydes use the ending –al. Select a parent chain containing the CHO carbon and include that carbon in the chain count. It is carbon 1, so CH3CH2CHO is propanal, not ethanal with an extra unnamed group. The one-to-six-carbon straight-chain aldehydes are methanal, ethanal, propanal, butanal, pentanal and hexanal. Branch locants are counted from the aldehyde end.

For example, CH3CH(CH3)CHO is 2-methylpropanal. Its parent has three carbons including CHO, while the methyl substituent adds a fourth to the whole molecule. Reconstructing the name gives the same carbon skeleton and ensures that an H remains attached to the carbonyl carbon. Merely naming the longest chain anywhere in a branched drawing can be wrong if that route omits the aldehyde group.

Ketones use –one and number the parent from the end giving the carbonyl carbon its lowest permitted locant. CH3COCH2CH2CH3 is pentan-2-one. CH3CH2COCH2CH3 is pentan-3-one. Both parents contain five carbons; the number identifies which carbon bears =O. In propanone there is one possible internal carbonyl position, so its usual simple name needs no locant.

To reverse a ketone name, draw the complete parent carbon chain first, number it and add a double bond to oxygen at the named carbon. Then fill the remaining carbon valencies with hydrogen. A terminal carbon bearing =O and H would instead give an aldehyde structure. Naming is therefore tied to connections, rather than a choice of ending based solely on a total atom count. Topic 4.5 uses this difference when identifying functional-group structural isomers.

### Composition from a carbonyl drawing

Count the carbonyl carbon as part of the carbon skeleton, then complete valencies at each carbon. Its double bond to O uses two contributions. In an aldehyde, one remaining contribution can be C–H and the other C–C; in a ketone both remaining contributions are C–C. Oxygen does not carry an implicit hydrogen in C=O. This is a common difference from the alcohol structures used earlier.

For CH3CH2CH2CHO, the hydrogen total is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, so butanal has C4H8O. For CH3COCH2CH3, the methyl groups supply six H, CH2 supplies two and the carbonyl carbon none, again giving C4H8O. Thus the same count can belong to an aldehyde or a ketone. The molecular composition does not establish the name or structure without further evidence.

In a skeletal drawing, a line to an explicit oxygen label is not an extra carbon position. The two lines of C=O represent a double bond between one carbon and one oxygen, not two oxygen atoms. Counting line strokes instead of labelled atoms and carbon positions would therefore give an impossible composition.

Use the saturated open-chain CnH2nO relationship as a check after the direct count. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms are separate answers: a molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula a ratio, and the connection representations show where atoms attach. Topic 1.1 covers calculating relative molecular mass from those counts. Here a calculated Mr can confirm arithmetic but cannot distinguish two isomers with equal composition.

### Preparing carbonyls from alcohols

Use acidified dichromate(VI), Cr2O7²−/H+, to oxidise primary and secondary alcohols. Ethanol gives ethanal in controlled oxidation: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O. The primary alcohol loses hydrogen from OH and from the same carbon to form C=O. Further oxidation can produce ethanoic acid, so limiting the intended stage and removing the volatile aldehyde as it forms helps obtain the aldehyde product.

A secondary alcohol instead gives a ketone. Propan-2-ol gives propanone: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O. Its OH-bearing carbon has one H available for removal and two carbon attachments. The product retains those two attachments at the carbonyl carbon. Oxidation of butan-2-ol similarly gives butan-2-one, preserving four carbons and the carbonyl position corresponding to the original OH-bearing carbon.

The oxidant's orange colour changes towards green as dichromate(VI) is reduced. That observation supports oxidation but does not on its own identify which carbonyl formed, since both primary and secondary alcohols can react. Use the starting alcohol's connections and product structure as well. A tertiary alcohol lacks H on its OH-bearing carbon and resists this ordinary mild carbonyl-forming route.

For a worked amount calculation, 0.100 mol propan-2-ol can give at most 0.100 mol propanone if oxidation is complete: the organic ratio is 1:1. Mr(propanone)=3(12.0)+6(1.0)+16.0=58.0, so the corresponding mass is 5.80 g. Actual isolated yield can be lower through incomplete reaction or loss during separation; neither changes the stoichiometric maximum calculated from the balanced equation. Topic 4.4 teaches the alcohol reaction map, and Topic 4.7 develops the carboxylic-acid endpoint of further primary oxidation.

1	# 4.7 Carboxylic acids and derivatives
2	
3	*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Carboxylic acids and derivatives — 4.7.1
8	
9	### Reading the carboxyl group
10	
11	A carboxylic acid contains the carboxyl group, –C(=O)OH. One oxygen is double-bonded to carbon and the other is single-bonded to that same carbon and to H. ### Linking ester properties to uses

Suitable esters are used as solvents because their polar ester group and carbon-containing portions can interact favourably with a range of organic solutes. Some also evaporate readily, allowing a dissolved coating or ingredient to remain after the solvent leaves. Ethyl ethanoate is an example of an ester solvent. Solubility depends on both the particular ester and solute; the presence of an ester linkage does not make a substance dissolve every material.

Many simple low-molecular-mass esters have characteristic pleasant or fruity odours. Enough molecules enter the vapour to reach the nose, making suitable compounds useful in perfume formulations and flavouring mixtures. The property belongs to particular structures and concentrations rather than to the mere word ester. Larger or differently substituted esters can have very different volatility and odour.

An original formulation comparison might specify that solvent A dissolves a resin and evaporates at a useful rate, while solvent B leaves the resin undissolved. Those observations support A for that stated task; they do not demonstrate that A is suitable for every formulation or direct consumption. Similarly, a pleasant smell alone does not establish that an unknown liquid is an ester or that it is appropriate as a food ingredient. Chemical identity and suitability require evidence beyond odour.

Distinguish a physical use from a reaction. Dissolving resin involves solute–solvent interactions; it does not imply ester hydrolysis. A perfume's scent likewise does not require breaking its ester bond during application. Topic 1.3 provides intermolecular-interaction reasoning, Topic 4.4 describes related solvent behaviour in alcohols, and the preceding section explains the deliberate aqueous acid or base settings that actually produce hydrolysis. Keep the useful property, application and relevant limitation linked in an explanation.
