1	# 5.1 Advanced practical skills
2	
3	*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Advanced practical skills — 5.1.1
8	
9	### Set up for the measurement you need
10	
11	Choose apparatus by the quantity and precision required. For a titration, clamp a burette vertically over a conical flask on a white tile. Rinse the burette with its intended solution, fill the tip and remove an air bubble before taking the initial reading. Remove the filling funnel so later drops cannot change the measured delivery. Use a pipette filler for the measured aliquot and keep the flask accessible for swirling.
12	
13	For gas collection, connect the reaction vessel to a freely moving gas syringe through airtight tubing. Support the syringe and check that the apparatus has enough capacity for the expected gas. Leaks lose product before measurement; a stuck plunger can obstruct collection. A thermometric setup instead needs an insulated vessel and a thermometer positioned in the liquid without pressing against the vessel wall.
14	
15	Sketch the actual measurement path before starting: what enters, what leaves and where the reading is made. Follow the supervised laboratory instructions and specified reagent handling. Apparatus that looks complete can still fail if its tip is unfilled, its joint leaks or its scale cannot be read.
16	
17	### Turn instructions into an ordered method
18	
19	Read the complete sequence before transferring a reagent. Mark which quantities are measured, which additions are gradual, which observations precede the next addition and where a fresh portion is required. A diagram can specify a connection or thermometer position that is not repeated in the prose. Match labels between the diagram and the written method before assembling it.
20	
21	“Add dropwise, then in excess” asks you to observe the initial change and then what happens when substantially more reagent is present. Record both stages. “Use a fresh portion” means take another portion of the original sample; it does not mean add a new reagent to a mixture already altered by the previous test. Otherwise a precipitate or gas may come from earlier additions rather than the unknown.
22	
23	For timed reactions, identify exactly when timing begins and the defined endpoint. For a titration, identify which liquid goes in the burette and which measured portion goes in the flask. If an instruction is unclear, resolve it with the supervisor before proceeding rather than silently swapping quantities. The resulting record should make it possible to connect each observation to the action that caused it.
24	
25	### Collect enough detail to discriminate
26	
27	Record what you actually see before interpreting it. “Pale blue precipitate, dissolving in excess to give a dark blue solution” describes three different features. “Blue” alone does not state whether the colour belongs to a solid or solution, or whether excess reagent changed it. Note effervescence, temperature change and whether a precipitate remains, where these are relevant to the specified test.
28	
29	For a temperature experiment, one reading before mixing and one much later may miss the highest temperature. Collect a baseline and frequent readings around the reaction, then continue long enough to reveal cooling. For a rate experiment, readings across the rising region are more informative than several readings taken after gas production has finished.
30	
31	Use the same descriptive level for comparable samples. If one result says “white precipitate insoluble in excess”, the other should also record initial precipitate and excess behaviour rather than merely “reacted”. Quantity comparisons such as more precipitate require comparable sample and reagent amounts. Topic 3.4 illustrates why a colour needs its material and reagent context; the qualitative task below supplies the specific reference results needed for its deductions.
32	
33	### Use each scale correctly
34	
35	Read a burette at eye level, using the appropriate meniscus for the liquid. Record two decimal places to the nearest 0.05 cm³ for the normal syllabus convention. A final reading 24.85 cm³ and initial reading 0.20 cm³ give a delivered titre of 24.65 cm³. The final reading alone is not the delivered volume unless the initial reading was zero.
36	
37	A volumetric pipette transfers a fixed calibrated volume. Use a filler, align the meniscus with the mark and allow delivery according to its calibration; do not force out a retained tip drop unless that pipette is designed for it. A measuring cylinder is less suitable when a small volume uncertainty matters. With a 1°C thermometer scale, normally estimate to 0.5°C; immerse the sensing part appropriately and wait for its response.
38	
39	Start a timing device at the defined reaction start and stop at the defined endpoint, not at an arbitrary convenient moment. Record balance readings using the displayed resolution. Raw precision comes from the measuring instrument and method, while the precision of a calculated result also depends on all inputs. Topic 1.1 supplies the unit conversions used after these readings are obtained.
40	
41	### Accuracy and consistency answer different questions
42	
43	Repeat measurements using the same endpoint definition and observation arrangement. In a titration, slow to dropwise addition near the expected endpoint, swirl thoroughly and compare the persistent indicator change against a white background. A rapid stream can overshoot even if the burette itself is read neatly. For a disappearing-cross reaction, use the same cross, viewing direction and criterion for disappearance in each run.
44	
45	Precision describes agreement between repeated readings and the resolution with which they are recorded. Accuracy describes closeness to the accepted value. Titres 24.65 and 24.70 cm³ are close to each other; this supports consistency but does not prove that the concentration calculated from them is accurate. A contaminated reagent or biased calibration can affect both similarly.
46	
47	Inspect the apparatus before explaining scatter. A bubble expelled from a burette tip during delivery can make the indicated volume exceed the volume actually delivered to the flask. Repeating the same faulty setup does not establish its accuracy. Use a consistent method, inspect plausible biases and report the readings rather than adjusting them to fit an expected result. Later evaluation sections distinguish removable bias from random variation.
48	
49	### Choose how many observations are needed
50	
51	Start from the question being answered. To distinguish two candidate ions, choose a supplied test whose predicted outcomes differ, then plan a confirmation if an ambiguous observation remains. Performing many unrelated additions to one tube can destroy the evidence needed for later deductions. Keep enough original material for fresh-portion comparisons and gas tests where appropriate.
52	
53	If both candidates produce a white precipitate with a particular reagent, that first observation does not distinguish them. Excess-reagent solubility or a second supplied reagent may do so. Conversely, once a discriminating observation has been obtained clearly and confirmed, repeating several chemically equivalent tests may waste time without testing a new explanation.
54	
55	For a continuous variable, collect enough distinct settings to reveal a trend and repeats to assess scatter. Three tightly clustered settings can be less informative about a curve than a wider pilot range with additional points near its changing region. The choice depends on available time, reagent and the experiment's response. State why the extra reading is needed: to resolve an ambiguity, confirm an endpoint or test a suspected anomaly. A numerical count of tests without that purpose is not a complete plan.
56	
57	### Distribute measurements across the response
58	
59	Choose the independent-variable range using a preliminary trial and the expected measurable response. Avoid settings at which the change is too small to read or too fast to time reliably. Within a useful range, regular spacing is a reasonable starting point, while extra points can be added where the response curves sharply or two fitted regions meet.
60	
61	For a concentration investigation, five distinct concentrations spanning a usable interval provide more information about proportionality than five repeated runs at one concentration. Repeats are valuable, but they answer a different question: scatter at a particular setting. Keep the total liquid volume constant by adding measured water when concentration is changed by dilution.
62	
63	For a thermometric titration, gather points on both sides of the maximum or intersection rather than stopping once warming is noticed. For a time series, use shorter intervals during the fastest change and longer intervals once the response slows, if the method permits. Record the actual chosen settings, not just “a range”. This lets another reader judge whether the graph covers enough of the phenomenon. The graphing unit below explains how the chosen range affects scale selection and the reliability of interpolation.
64	
65	### Decide when a reading represents the process
66	
67	A useful waiting time depends on what is being measured. Before a thermal reaction, allow starting solutions to approach the same chosen temperature and check a stable baseline. After mixing, record frequently enough to capture the rise and subsequent cooling. Waiting several minutes for a single “stable final” temperature can miss the maximum because heat is already leaving the solution.
68	
69	Near a titration endpoint, add a small amount, swirl and wait long enough to decide whether the colour persists under the stated method. A redox endpoint may require a pale colour to remain for a specified period; the persistence criterion belongs with the observation. Do not substitute an intense colour caused by overshooting.
70	
71	For gas collection, continue until no further measurable increase occurs over an appropriate interval, while recognising that a leak can also produce an apparent plateau. For slow dissolution or precipitation, allow the instructed time before judging solubility. A preliminary run can establish a sensible sampling interval. Explain the choice through the response time or transient change, rather than treating a longer wait as an automatic improvement. In a recorded method, state both the interval between readings and the criterion used to stop collecting them.
72	
73	### Repeat where it improves the evidence
74	
75	Use a rough titration to locate the endpoint, then obtain careful repeat titres. For this syllabus, concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³. Mark the closest suitable pair used in the mean and exclude the rough value. If careful titres remain inconsistent, inspect delivery, endpoint recognition and apparatus before calculating a mean that hides the disagreement.
76	
77	For example, careful titres 24.65, 24.70 and 25.10 cm³ support choosing the first two. Their mean is 24.675 cm³; retain that value during subsequent calculation and report at a justified precision. Investigate the third value as a possible overshoot or other anomalous run, recording the reason rather than erasing it from the original table.
78	
79	Repeats also apply to qualitative work: an unexpected precipitate may need a fresh-portion test to check contamination. Replicating a rate run at selected settings helps assess timing scatter. Repeats do not remove a constant scale offset or restore heat already lost systematically. State which uncertainty the repeat can address and preserve individual readings so the observed spread remains visible. The recording unit below shows how raw and selected data can occupy one coherent table.
80	
81	### Confirm the proposed identity
82	
83	Effervescence shows gas production, not gas identity. Use a suitable fresh gas sample with the supplied reference test: carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, ammonia turns damp red litmus blue, oxygen relights a glowing splint, and hydrogen gives a pop with a lighted splint under the supervised procedure. Do not apply a flame test indiscriminately to an unknown gas mixture. The task specifies which gas test is appropriate.
84	
85	For an ion, select confirmation that addresses the remaining alternative. A pale blue precipitate followed by dissolution in excess ammonia to a dark blue solution is more discriminating than the word “blue” alone. A carbonate proposal gains support when the gas produced with dilute acid is confirmed as CO2 rather than merely observed bubbling.
86	
87	Keep observation and deduction in separate table columns. If the supplied notes do not distinguish two possible ions with the chosen test, report the ambiguity and choose a different permitted comparison rather than claiming certainty. Fresh portions help avoid attributing an observation to a reagent used earlier. Topic 3.4 covers relevant halogen chemistry, but the purpose here is to use the provided notes to select and interpret observations, not memorise an unsupported list of tests.
88	
89	### Select reagents from a candidate table
90	
91	Read the supplied candidate results before choosing a reagent. Aluminium and zinc both give white precipitates soluble in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide, so that comparison alone cannot separate them. With aqueous ammonia, the aluminium precipitate remains in excess whereas zinc's dissolves. That difference supplies a useful second test on fresh portions.
92	
93	Likewise a barium-nitrate precipitate can require acid treatment to distinguish sulfate from sulfite using the supplied notes. A persistent white precipitate after nitric acid supports sulfate; dissolution supports the sulfite alternative. Use the order and reagent specified in the question. Selecting a reagent because it produces any visible reaction is insufficient when both candidates share that reaction.
94	
95	Write a small decision table: candidate, first addition, excess or follow-up, predicted difference. Then perform only the permitted comparisons and record the actual outcomes. If an observation is faint, use comparable sample amounts, a clean background and fresh apparatus to check it. Do not convert an unresolved pale precipitate into a confident identity merely to complete the table. The practical qualitative task includes its reference outcomes so the reasoning remains reconstructible offline.
96	
97	---
98	
99	## Advanced practical skills — 5.1.2
100	
101	### Keep one coherent results table
102	
103	Prepare one table in which each trial keeps its associated readings together. A titration table can use trial columns with rows for initial reading, final reading and titre, or trial rows with separate quantity columns. Either orientation must make it unambiguous which final reading belongs to which initial reading. Include units in headings and identify the rough trial.
104	
105	An original example is shown below. The final-minus-initial calculation gives each titre; the two careful values are selected for the mean.
106	
107	| Trial | Initial reading / cm³ | Final reading / cm³ | Titre / cm³ |
108	|---|---:|---:|---:|
109	| Rough | 0.00 | 25.30 | 25.30 |
110	| 1 | 0.20 | 24.85 | 24.65 |
111	| 2 | 0.10 | 24.80 | 24.70 |
112	
113	The careful titres differ by 0.05 cm³, within the 0.10 cm³ concordance criterion. Preserve the rough reading even though it is not averaged. For qualitative tests, use the same idea of alignment: each reagent addition needs its observation and inference beside it, rather than collecting unlabelled colour descriptions elsewhere on the page.
114	
115	### Prepare a table before starting
116	
117	Design the table after reading the method and before collecting data. Include trial or sample identifiers, raw quantities and any derived column needed for the question. Leave enough space for repeats and unexpected observations. A cramped table can turn a careful result into an ambiguous entry, particularly when colour, solid formation and excess behaviour must all be described.
118	
119	For a gas-volume time series, prepare Time / s and Gas volume / cm³ columns. For a thermometric experiment add a note marking when mixing occurred so that baseline and post-mixing readings are distinguishable. For titration include both initial and final burette readings instead of reserving space for the titre alone.
120	
121	Before using a prepared table, check a sample subtraction or unit conversion to confirm that the necessary columns exist. For instance, initial 1.10 cm³ and final 25.75 cm³ need a Titre / cm³ cell for 24.65. Do not write an expected value into a raw-reading cell before observing it. Preparation organises evidence; it does not authorise inventing data that an experiment did not produce.
122	
123	### Separate measurements from calculations and conclusions
124	
125	Raw readings are directly observed quantities, such as mass before and after a reaction or initial and final temperature. Derived values combine those readings, such as mass loss or temperature rise. A conclusion interprets them chemically. Give these roles separate labelled columns or clearly separated table sections so that a reader can check each step.
126	
127	For a balance experiment, include Initial mass / g, Final mass / g and Mass loss / g. If the readings are 52.64 and 52.20 g, the derived loss is 0.44 g. The statement that gas escaped is an interpretation requiring the method and chemical reaction; it is not another balance reading. For qualitative analysis, “white precipitate remains in excess” is an observation, while “consistent with Al3+ among these candidates” is a deduction.
128	
129	Retaining raw data allows a correction to be traced. If a subtraction is wrong, fix the derived value rather than changing the observed masses to fit it. The thermometric and rates tasks below use raw and derived columns together; Topic 2.1 supplies the energy relationship used after a measured temperature rise has been established.
130	
131	### Headings carry quantity and unit
132	
133	Write headings such as Time / s, Temperature / °C, Volume / cm³ or Concentration / mol dm−3. “Volume (cm³)” is also clear. A bare unit does not say what was measured, and a bare quantity leaves its scale undefined. Place the unit in the heading so numerical entries can be read consistently without repeating a symbol in each cell.
134	
135	Use an unambiguous quantity name. If a table contains both time and temperature, a column labelled t is unclear; spell out the quantities or define distinct symbols. For derived columns, the unit may differ from the raw one. A reciprocal time column is 1/time / s−1, while a time interval remains in seconds.
136	
137	For example, times 100.0 and 50.0 s give reciprocal values 0.01000 and 0.02000 s−1. Writing those under Time / s would mislabel the calculation even though the arithmetic is correct. Unit conversion should also be explicit: a measured volume in cm³ divided by 1000 gives dm³ for use with concentration in mol dm−3. Topic 1.1 explains why matching these units matters for amounts of substance.
138	
139	### Record instrument precision
140	
141	Use the resolution and reading convention of the apparatus rather than a number of decimal places chosen to look impressive. Normal burette readings here use two decimal places with the last digit 0 or 5. A 1°C-scale thermometer normally supports 0.5°C steps in the stated syllabus practice. Balance readings should retain the displayed decimal places consistently within a raw-data column.
142	
143	If a balance resolves 0.01 g, write 2.40 g rather than 2.4 g when that is the actual display. The trailing zero records resolution; it does not change the mass. Subtracting 2.40 from 2.85 g gives 0.45 g, retaining the hundredth-gram place. A calculated quantity may later need a significant-figure decision, which is a separate issue.
144	
145	Consistency also applies to words. Describe the initial precipitate, its colour and excess-reagent behaviour for each comparable sample. “White solid remained” and “dissolved to a colourless solution” are more comparable than “white” and “nothing”. Record changes as they occur instead of relying on memory after several similar tubes have been tested.
146	
147	### Show the route to the answer
148	
149	Begin a calculation with the relationship required. For a concentration calculation, use n=cV with V in dm³ when c is in mol dm−3. State the reaction's mole ratio before converting from one reactant to the other. Then calculate the requested amount, concentration or mass. Carry enough intermediate digits to avoid premature rounding and include units in the final answer.
150	
151	For 24.675 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm−3 NaOH, V=0.024675 dm³ and n=0.100×0.024675=0.0024675 mol. If it neutralises a 25.00 cm³ HCl aliquot in a 1:1 reaction, c(HCl)=0.0024675/0.02500=0.0987 mol dm−3 to three significant figures. The mean titre remains unrounded until the final step.
152	
153	Show reasoning similarly in qualitative work. A white precipitate soluble in excess NaOH fits both Al3+ and Zn2+ from the supplied notes; a fresh-portion ammonia test then distinguishes the remaining candidates by excess solubility. The intermediate alternatives matter. An unexplained final identity hides whether the observation actually discriminated it. Topic 2.2 supplies balanced redox ratios used in the redox titration task.
154	
155	### Round after the calculation
156	
157	Read the precision of the supplied quantities before deciding how many significant figures to report. The syllabus permits calculated results at the same number of significant figures as the least accurate measured input, or one more where justified. Do not add precision by multiplying several rounded values. Keep guard digits in working and round the final result clearly.
158	
159	The number 0.0500 has three significant figures, while 0.05 has one. A mass 5.00 g has three; a raw balance reading's decimal places still depend on the display. For a measured 0.100 mol dm−3 standard and titre 24.675 cm³ used internally, a resulting concentration 0.0987 mol dm−3 appropriately reflects three significant figures in the standard.
160	
161	In a subtraction, absolute reading resolution matters: temperatures 23.0 and 29.5°C give a rise 6.5°C, not an artificially precise 6.500. A later enthalpy based on that rise should not claim five reliable significant figures. State the chosen precision with the final answer. Exact coefficients in a balanced equation do not restrict significant figures because they count the stoichiometric ratio rather than represent uncertain measurements.
162	
163	---
164	
165	## Advanced practical skills — 5.1.3
166	
167	### Choose a useful display
168	
169	Use a table for observations linked to samples or reagent additions. It preserves the exact words and makes initial and excess behaviour easy to compare. For a continuous measured response such as gas volume against time, a graph reveals a changing gradient more clearly than a sequence of numbers alone. Keep the raw table as well, because a graph does not replace the original measurements.
170	
171	Choose the display according to the question. A straight-line calibration graph can help estimate an unknown concentration, while a precipitate's colour and solubility are better shown in a labelled observation table. A bar chart can suit categories; it is less useful than a continuous plot when the independent variable varies continuously and intermediate values have meaning.
172	
173	Before plotting, decide what feature the display should reveal: trend, gradient, intercept, comparison or anomaly. This prevents a decorative graph from obscuring the calculation. The rates task uses both measured times and a reciprocal-time graph. Topic 2.4 explains the chemistry behind the changing rates, while this unit focuses on making the measured evidence readable.
174	
175	### Choose variables and readable scales
176	
177	Put the chosen independent variable on the horizontal axis and the measured dependent variable on the vertical axis unless a specified relationship calls for a different arrangement. Label both with quantity and unit. Gas volume / cm³ against Time / s means the vertical coordinate is volume, not a second time reading.
178	
179	Choose regular increments that are easy to subdivide, such as 1, 2 or 5 units per major grid interval. Use enough of both dimensions to distinguish the points and draw a gradient triangle. A graph occupying a tiny corner makes interpolation and slope less reliable. A numerical axis need not start at zero when a different origin makes the required trend clearer, but show the chosen range honestly.
180	
181	For times from 0 to 100 s and volumes from 0 to 60 cm³, a horizontal range 0–100 and vertical range 0–60 is sensible. The scale should include the data rather than stopping short of the last point. Recheck that equal physical distances represent equal numerical intervals. Topic 5.1.4 applies these displays to unknown values and control-variable evaluation.
182	
183	### Plot positions rather than approximate impressions
184	
185	Locate each coordinate separately using the stated scales, then make a fine cross or another small clear symbol. A large blob can conceal whether a point is correctly placed. Check that each raw-table row has one matching point unless the graph intentionally uses a derived value such as a mean or reciprocal time.
186	
187	If one horizontal division represents 10 s and one vertical division 5 cm³, a reading at 25 s and 32 cm³ belongs halfway between 20 and 30 s and two units above 30 cm³. Do not round it to the nearest major intersection simply to make plotting easier. If two points overlap, annotate their multiplicity or retain the table so the repeats remain known.
188	
189	Check extreme points and suspected anomalies first because a misplaced point can distort the fitted trend. If an observation is genuinely anomalous, ring or label it and explain how it is treated. Do not move it towards the line, delete it silently or alter the raw table. A correctly plotted unexpected result can be useful evidence about the experiment.
190	
191	### Fit the trend supported by the data
192	
193	Inspect the plotted pattern before choosing a straight line or smooth curve. A roughly linear pattern supports a best-fit straight line with points distributed on both sides. A changing gradient can require a smooth curve. Joining successive measured points with sharp corners treats random scatter as if it were a physical change in the underlying process.
194	
195	For a gas-volume curve, reaction often slows as a reactant is consumed. A curve can rise steeply and then level off. A straight line across the whole run would hide that changing rate. Conversely, a linear calibration should not be replaced by an arbitrary curved path just to touch each point.
196	
197	Use a fine, continuous line and keep excluded anomalies visible. Do not force a line through the origin because the axes happen to cross there; an intercept can reveal a baseline contribution or systematic offset. If a theoretical model predicts zero response at zero input, consider whether the measured uncertainty supports that constraint. The next sections explain how transformations, slopes and intercepts turn the fitted trend into a quantitative interpretation.
198	
199	### Use a justified linear treatment
200	
201	Choose transformed variables because a model predicts a relationship, not because a straight line looks convenient. For repeated reactions timed to the same small extent, reciprocal time can act as a rate proxy. Plotting 1/time against concentration can then test proportionality over the range studied, provided the endpoint, temperature, total volume and other relevant factors are matched.
202	
203	For concentrations 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80 and 1.00 mol dm−3, illustrative endpoint times 100.0, 50.0, 33.3, 25.0 and 20.0 s give reciprocal times approximately 0.0100, 0.0200, 0.0300, 0.0400 and 0.0500 s−1. This is nearly linear with slope 0.0500 s−1 per mol dm−3 and intercept near zero.
204	
205	![Original reciprocal-time data and linear fit](assets/8224-practical-linear-rate.png)
206	
207	The reciprocal is not automatically a measured initial rate in mol per second. It is a comparison based on the fixed endpoint; a changing endpoint invalidates it. State the model, transformation and units before using the fitted line. Topic 2.4 provides the kinetic principles, while the practical rates task asks you to test the transformation with original data.
208	
209	### Interpret slope and intercept physically
210	
211	For a straight-line model y=mx+c, m is the gradient and c the vertical intercept. Choose two well-separated coordinates on the fitted line, not necessarily two raw points, and calculate Δy/Δx. Use a triangle spanning at least half the useful line where possible. The units are vertical-axis units divided by horizontal-axis units.
212	
213	If a volume–time line passes through (10 s, 8 cm³) and (90 s, 40 cm³), its gradient is (40−8)/(90−10)=0.400 cm³ s−1. Extending that line to zero time gives an intercept of 4 cm³. The gradient describes the modelled volume increase per second; the intercept describes the extrapolated volume at zero time and may reflect an initial reading offset or an actual initial volume, depending on the method.
214	
215	Do not interpret an intercept by naming its number alone. Explain what zero on the horizontal axis means in that experiment. If zero lies far outside the measured range, the extrapolated value can be uncertain even when the measured points fit well. Report the coordinates used so another reader can check both the arithmetic and the physical meaning.
216	
217	### Tangent rate and meaningful area
218	
219	On a curved volume–time graph, draw a tangent at the specified time and calculate its gradient using a large triangle on that tangent. This estimates the instantaneous volume-production rate there. A line connecting the beginning and end of a long interval instead gives an average rate and can miss the changing local slope.
220	
221	An original model is V=60(1−exp(−time/40)) cm³ with time in seconds. At 40 s the volume is about 37.9 cm³ and its tangent gradient about 0.552 cm³ s−1. The tangent can be read using widely separated coordinates near (0 s,15.9 cm³) and (80 s,60.0 cm³). The curve itself is not that straight line.
222	
223	![Original volume curve and tangent at40s](assets/8224-practical-tangent.png)
224	
225	An area under a rate–time graph has units of amount or volume and can represent accumulated production. An area under a volume–time graph instead has units cm³ s and is not the total gas volume. Check units and the physical model before assigning meaning. Topic 2.4 supplies rate concepts; this skill connects a graph construction with the particular rate requested.
226	
227	---
228	
229	## Advanced practical skills — 5.1.4
230	
231	### Support patterns with measured values
232	
233	State what changes as the independent variable increases, quoting values that show the pattern. For gas production, “volume rises from 0.0 to 37.9 cm³ in the first 40 s and then to 51.9 cm³ by 80 s” is more informative than “it increases quickly”. Equal time intervals here give smaller volume gains later, supporting a decreasing average rate.
234	
235	Distinguish rate from final amount. Two runs can reach the same plateau at different speeds if the same limiting amount reacts. A steeper initial curve does not by itself establish more total gas. Likewise a larger final volume does not prove faster reaction if the experiment used more reactant.
236	
237	Use the table or graph's actual numbers and units. Describe the measured range before extending to a broader claim. If a point departs from the pattern, identify it rather than hiding it in a vague statement such as “mostly proportional”. The supplied qualitative notes can support patterns across samples too, but use comparable reagent amounts before claiming that one precipitate quantity is larger. Topic 2.4 links a declining gas-production rate to the changing reacting system.
238	
239	### Summarise the distinguishing evidence
240	
241	A useful summary selects the observations relevant to the question while preserving their detail. For a cation comparison, record initial precipitate colour and whether it dissolves in excess reagent. For an anion comparison, include gas evolution and the result of its confirmation. These are different kinds of evidence and should not be collapsed into the word “reaction”.
242	
243	For example, “A gave a white precipitate with NaOH, soluble in excess, but its ammonia precipitate remained in excess; B dissolved in excess with both reagents” summarises a discriminating pattern from the supplied notes. It does not yet replace the interpretation step that assigns candidate identities.
244	
245	State negative observations as carefully as positive ones. “No visible precipitate after the specified addition and observation time” is clearer than leaving a blank, which could mean that the test was not done. If a solution colour obscures a small solid, acknowledge that limitation and improve the comparison. An honest summary can retain ambiguity where the collected observations do not separate the candidates. The qualitative task asks for both the observed pattern and the reason it supports a particular conclusion.
246	
247	### Read an unknown from coordinates
248	
249	Use the fitted relationship rather than choosing the nearest raw point. To estimate an unknown concentration from a measured response, move from that response to the calibration line and then to the concentration axis. Show the construction or state the coordinates so the reading can be checked. Keep the unit associated with the quantity, not just the numerical coordinate.
250	
251	For a calibration S=20.0c+0.10, where S is a stated dimensionless signal and c is in mol dm−3, S=0.70 gives c=(0.70−0.10)/20.0=0.0300 mol dm−3. Subtracting the intercept matters; dividing 0.70 directly by 20.0 would ignore the baseline signal. If the calibration was measured from 0.0100 to 0.0500 mol dm−3, this is interpolation.
252	
253	A response corresponding to 0.0800 mol dm−3 would require extrapolation beyond that range. Report that dependence rather than presenting it as equally well supported. A new measured standard nearer the unknown can test the model there. The graphing unit's slope and intercept rules therefore contribute directly to finding unknowns, rather than being isolated numerical exercises.
254	
255	### Calculate from selected comparable data
256	
257	Identify which repeats measure the same quantity under the same settings. For titres, use a suitable concordant pair and show which are selected. For 24.65 and 24.70 cm³, the mean is (24.65+24.70)/2=24.675 cm³. A rough value is used to guide the endpoint, not included just because it is another number in the table.
258	
259	Convert the mean to the volume unit required by concentration before calculating moles. Then use the balanced equation's ratio. In a redox titration, one manganate(VII) ion can react with five Fe2+ ions in acid; treating that as a 1:1 ratio would overwhelm a small improvement in burette precision. Topic 2.2 gives the balanced electron accounting.
260	
261	When averaging rate runs, state whether you average endpoint times and then invert or calculate and average reciprocal times; these are not exactly identical for scattered data. Follow the task's requested method and retain individual values. A mean without the spread can conceal inconsistent measurements. Report a calculated conclusion at a precision justified by the measured quantities and distinguish a theoretical amount from an experimentally recovered one.
262	
263	### Calculate the gradient you actually drew
264	
265	Mark two coordinates on the straight line or tangent used for the interpretation. Form a triangle large enough that small reading uncertainties are a limited fraction of its height and width. Calculate change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity, preserving the sign where it has meaning. State the unit derived from both axes.
266	
267	For the volume tangent near 40 s, coordinates (0 s,15.9 cm³) and (80 s,60.0 cm³) give (60.0−15.9)/80=0.55125 cm³ s−1, appropriately about 0.55 cm³ s−1 from those graph readings. This is compatible with the underlying model's approximately 0.552 rate. It is not the average rate from time zero to 80 s on the curve.
268	
269	For a decreasing mass–time graph, a negative gradient indicates decreasing measured mass; its magnitude can describe mass-loss rate if that is the requested quantity. Do not silently remove a negative sign without stating the physical convention. If the graph is a transformed plot, use its transformed units rather than assigning a familiar rate unit automatically.
270	
271	### Evaluate whether a control worked
272	
273	Identify variables other than the chosen independent one that can affect the response. In a concentration–rate experiment these can include temperature, total volume, particle size, amount of solid and mixing method. State how each is kept comparable and what measurement checks that it remained so. A list of names without a method does not demonstrate control.
274	
275	If successive reaction mixtures start at 20.0, 22.0 and 25.0°C as concentration increases, temperature is confounded with concentration. Faster reaction could partly reflect warmer mixtures. A thermostatically controlled bath and measured starting temperatures reduce that ambiguity. Merely using the same room does not guarantee the liquid temperatures match.
276	
277	When diluting a reagent, replace the removed reagent volume with measured water to keep the total volume constant. Keep other reactants in the intended excess and use the same endpoint. Evaluate actual values where available: a temperature spread smaller than the stated measurement uncertainty may be less concerning than a systematic several-degree rise. Topic 2.4 explains why temperature affects rate; the practical judgement asks whether that effect has been isolated from the intended comparison.
278	
279	### Find the error that matters most
280	
281	Start with the measured result and trace what could bias it. In an uninsulated calorimetry experiment, heat transferred to the surroundings lowers the observed temperature rise, so a calculation attributing all reaction heat to the solution underestimates the magnitude of an exothermic enthalpy. In gas collection, a leak can reduce measured volume. These are specific mechanisms with a plausible direction.
282	
283	Compare the likely size of competing effects. If temperature rise is 4.0°C and uncertainty in the rise is 1.0°C, that contribution is much larger proportionally than a 0.01 g uncertainty in a 50.00 g mass. Focus an improvement on the larger contribution while recognising that heat loss may add a separate systematic effect.
284	
285	“Human error” does not explain how a result changes. A variable delay in starting a timer, a consistent parallax direction and an overrun endpoint are different errors and need different remedies. Avoid claiming a direction where the method does not establish one: variable judging of a disappearing cross can scatter readings either side. Support significance with data, apparatus resolution or a clear description of material lost or energy transferred.
286	
287	### Quantify uncertainty explicitly
288	
289	State the uncertainty model used. If each burette reading has an assumed uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, a delivered volume obtained from two readings has a simple maximum uncertainty ±0.10 cm³. For a 25.00 cm³ titre, the percentage is 0.10/25.00×100=0.400 percent. This is a conservative reading-uncertainty estimate, not a measurement of actual experimental error against a known truth.
290	
291	For thermometer readings each uncertain by ±0.5°C, a temperature difference has a simple maximum uncertainty ±1.0°C. A measured rise 6.5°C therefore has about 15 percent uncertainty by this model. A rise 2.0°C would have a much larger 50 percent for the same instrument. Increasing the measured change within a valid experiment can reduce the relative contribution.
292	
293	Do not invent apparatus uncertainty from the number of written decimal places when a calibration or supplied value is available. Use the stated instrument information. Separate random spread, calibration uncertainty and systematic heat transfer where relevant; one percentage does not automatically include all of them. Topic 1.1 supplies the arithmetic of ratios, while this practical skill requires deciding what uncertainty belongs in the numerator.
294	
295	### Distinguish scatter from bias
296	
297	Random errors vary unpredictably between repeats and can make values fall above or below the underlying result. Repeating and averaging comparable readings can reduce their effect on the mean. Systematic errors arise from a consistent bias, such as a calibration offset or a method that persistently loses heat before it is measured. Repeating the same biased method does not remove that bias.
298	
299	Consider a thermometer that reads 1.0°C too high at both temperatures. True readings 22.0 and 28.0°C become 23.0 and 29.0°C, but the difference remains 6.0°C. The constant additive offset cancels in that difference. It still makes an individual absolute temperature wrong, and a changing or scale-factor error would not necessarily cancel.
300	
301	A burette zero reading is also not itself a problem if both initial and final readings are taken correctly and subtracted. By contrast, a bubble changing during delivery can alter the relation between scale difference and liquid reaching the flask. Analyse the measured difference rather than assuming any offset must change it. An evaluation identifies both the kind of error and how the specific calculation responds.
302	
303	### Draw a conclusion with its evidence
304	
305	State the answer to the investigation's question, then cite the observation or calculation that supports it. An exothermic conclusion can cite a measured positive temperature rise after accounting for the baseline. A concentration conclusion gives its numerical value and unit from the selected titre and balanced reaction. A qualitative conclusion identifies the candidate pattern used.
306	
307	If the supplied choices are Al3+ and Zn2+, a precipitate remaining in excess ammonia can separate them after the shared NaOH behaviour. Without those choices and reference information, the same brief observation may not identify a unique ion. Keep the conclusion tied to the evidence actually available.
308	
309	Express uncertainty or ambiguity where it affects the outcome. Two concentrations differing by less than their combined plausible measurement spread may not support a claimed change. A poorly controlled temperature comparison does not establish concentration as the sole cause of faster reaction. The conclusion should not introduce observations that were never recorded or extend automatically to untested materials. The six integrated tasks below require a conclusion after the working so that the numerical and observational chain remains visible.
310	
311	### Test a stated hypothesis rather than a vague expectation
312	
313	Translate the hypothesis into a measurable prediction. “Reciprocal endpoint time is proportional to concentration” predicts a straight 1/time–concentration graph through the origin within uncertainty, when the same small endpoint and other relevant settings are matched. A straight line with a clearly nonzero intercept would not establish that exact proportionality, even if the response increases with concentration.
314	
315	Compare the fit with scatter and control-variable evidence. Measurements near a straight trend support the model over the tested range; they do not demonstrate it for arbitrary concentrations, temperatures or reaction extents. Quote a relevant pair of values or the slope and intercept rather than simply writing “the hypothesis is correct”.
316	
317	Use the supported model to make a stated prediction. With a fitted relationship 1/time=0.0500c, c=0.50 mol dm−3 gives 1/time=0.0250 s−1 and time=40.0 s. This is interpolation if the tested range spans 0.20–1.00 mol dm−3. At a much higher concentration, additional measurements would be needed before assuming the same relationship remains valid. Topic 2.4 explains why a controlled comparison matters for the kinetic inference.
318	
319	### Connect evidence to a mechanism
320	
321	After describing a result, explain it using an appropriate chemical or physical principle. A falling gas-production gradient can follow reactant consumption reducing the frequency of successful collisions. A temperature rise after neutralisation reflects energy released overall and transferred to the solution. A precipitate dissolving in excess reagent requires the relevant supplied chemistry, rather than an inference from colour alone.
322	
323	For example, if two runs have the same limiting amount and final gas volume but one is initially faster at higher temperature, the result can be explained through a greater fraction of collisions exceeding the activation barrier. Do not say that a catalyst raises the temperature or changes the equilibrium yield merely because it speeds the reaction. Match the explanation to the variable actually changed.
324	
325	Keep assumptions visible. A solution-temperature calculation usually assumes a density and heat capacity, and may neglect the vessel's heat capacity. Its numerical enthalpy therefore depends on that model as well as on the observations. Topic 2.1 supplies energy accounting and Topic 2.4 rate theory. In practical work these ideas explain why a particular pattern occurred and why a limitation can change the calculated result.
326	
327	### Make improvements that address the cause
328	
329	Pair each improvement with the limitation it addresses. Insulation and a lid reduce heat transfer to the surroundings; checking gas joints reduces leakage; a thermostatic bath helps control reaction temperature. A longer, readable gradient triangle reduces the fractional effect of coordinate-reading uncertainty. These are practical changes with an identifiable connection to the result.
330	
331	Repeating a timed run addresses random scatter, while checking calibration addresses a persistent scale bias. A more finely marked measuring device is useful when reading resolution is a significant contribution, but it does not recover gas that escaped through a leaking stopper. Likewise a digital thermometer alone does not remove heat absorbed by an unaccounted vessel.
332	
333	Describe the change clearly enough that another student could implement it. “Be more accurate” gives no action. “Read the meniscus at eye level with a fixed white background” specifies an observational change. If an improvement introduces another effect, consider it: changing reactant volumes to increase a temperature rise can also change the limiting amount, so the amount calculation must be updated. State which quantity becomes more reliable and why the proposed change is realistic for the experiment.
334	
335	### Extend the investigation to answer a new question
336	
337	Begin with the new question explicitly. If the original work studies concentration and rate, an extension might ask how temperature changes the same endpoint rate while concentration is held fixed. Choose several temperatures in a usable range, equilibrate mixtures in a bath, measure starting temperatures, repeat timed runs and keep the amount, total volume and endpoint unchanged.
338	
339	That is different from repeating the original concentration experiment to reduce scatter. Repetition can improve evidence for the original question but does not by itself answer how temperature affects the response. Similarly, adding a lid to reduce heat loss is an improvement unless the new question is specifically about heat transfer under different insulation arrangements.
340	
341	State the proposed independent variable, dependent measurement and controls. Explain what pattern would answer the question and how comparable data will be displayed. If investigating a different catalyst, keep its specified amount or exposed area comparable as appropriate and distinguish rate effects from final amount. Avoid extensions phrased merely as “try other chemicals”: different reactants can change stoichiometry and the phenomenon being compared. A useful extension is a small, testable investigation with a clear connection to the evidence already collected.
342
